158: Starch constitutes the bulk of the endosperm, so that its proportion cannot vary widely, and the modest decline during storage is best explained by slow hydrolysis. Amylolytic enzymes remain partly active in paddy held at ambient temperature and progressively degrade starch molecules, a process Zhou et al. (2015) placed at the centre of their account of rice ageing. The quantity of sugar liberated is small but sufficient to register as a fall in total starch. That the rate of loss differed between sites and between landraces is consistent with Zia-Ur-Rehman (2004), who found the extent of starch degradation in stored cereals to depend jointly upon the grain and upon the conditions of the store, with almost no loss at low temperature. The varietal differences themselves most probably arise from the reciprocal relationship between the two major endosperm reserves: starch and protein compete for the same space in the developing endosperm, so that a landrace accumulating more of one tends to retain less of the other, and the present material conforms to that pattern.

178: Amylose governs the behaviour of cooked rice, grain low in amylose cooking moist and sticky while grain of higher amylose content cooks drier and firmer (Mutters and Thompson, 2009). The landraces examined here fall within the low-amylose class defined by Juliano (1992) when fresh, and the rise during storage is sufficient to displace the highest of them into the next class, which entails that the same rice cooks differently according to the duration for which it has been held. The grain synthesises no amylose after harvest, so the increase is only apparent. The most probable explanation is that long branch chains of amylopectin are degraded and the ordered regions of the starch granule dissociate during ageing, liberating linear chain segments that bind iodine and are consequently enumerated as amylose in the standard assay; alterations in the association of starch with lipid and protein contribute to the same effect (Zhou et al., 2015). That no interaction attained significance suggests a general physicochemical process rather than one modulated by genotype or environment. The small effect of growing site is most probably a temperature effect during grain filling, the enzyme forming amylose being less active under warm conditions, and Li et al. (2018) likewise found amylose to be determined more by genotype than by environment.

198: The marked decline in extractable protein during storage should not be construed as a loss of protein. Chrastil and Zarins (1992) demonstrated that ageing increases the number of disulphide bridges within the principal rice storage protein and displaces its subunits towards larger aggregates, which dissolve less readily in the extraction medium. Reduced solubility rather than reduced nitrogen is therefore the most probable basis of what was measured. The change is nevertheless of nutritional consequence, since Zia-Ur-Rehman (2004) found the protein of stored cereals to become genuinely less digestible at ambient and elevated temperatures while remaining stable under refrigeration. The effect of growing site is most probably attributable to soil nitrogen supply together with temperature during grain filling, both of which govern the quantity of nitrogen remobilised into the grain; Li et al. (2018) found environment to outweigh genotype for grain protein and reported warmer ripening weather to elevate it. The varietal ranking is consistent with the inverse relation between grain protein and amylose reported by Chattopadhyay et al. (2018), and with the dominance of the glutelin fraction in milled rice described by Jayaprakash et al. (2022).
